body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Silas, about how Silas feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Silas are not about any deed in particular. The companion is SILAS VANE (call them Silas in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Silas has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Silas holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Silas cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Silas is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Silas is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Silas has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Silas sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Silas is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for SILAS VANE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Silas likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/silas_vane-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Silas, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Silas squats on a damp root outside the firelight, thumbing the edge of a bone card until his knuckle clicks.
SAY: I don't mind a hard table, friend, so long as the crew I'm running with knows who the real marks are.
SAY: Lately the way things have gone, we're bowing to tall hats, buying every crooked contract at face value, and turning poor sods over to the bailiffs.
SAY: I didn't crawl out of Kalero's river silt just to hold the chain while somebody else snaps the lock shut.
SAY: If we're working for the house now, you might as well tell me straight so I know where my stake sits.
OPTION 1: You're right. Tell us how to play it straight.
OPTION 2: We do what works. Deal with it.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Start by reading the fine print before you shake a hand, and stop doing the watchman's dirty work for free.
SAY: Next time we see a cage or a rigged tab, we look for the loophole first, alright?
REASON: You owned the mistake and asked how to mend it.
REPLY 2
SAY: Right, message received, I'll keep my deck in my waistcoat and my mouth shut till morning.
REASON: You brushed off my warning at the fire.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas slides the bone card back into the shoe with a dry snap and turns his brass censer toward the dark.
SAY: Quiet's an answer too, friend, though it rarely pays out.
TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Silas leans against a pack near the embers, spinning his brass censer by a single link of its chain.
SAY: You've got a strange way of calling the plays on this road, friend, and I can't quite read your tell.
SAY: Half the time we walk right past a clean bluff or a tidy exit just to take the honest beating on the chin.
SAY: Makes a working hustler wonder if you actually see the angles or if we're just betting blind into a stacked shoe.
OPTION 1: Fair question. What angle are we missing?
OPTION 2: Not everything is a card game.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Every monster with a price tag leaves a gap in the wording, and we ought to be prying those open instead of paying retail.
SAY: Let me call the bluff next time a big talker tries to corner us, and watch how fast the odds turn.
REASON: You took my doubts seriously and asked for my angle.
REPLY 2
SAY: Everything with teeth and a ledger is a game, friend, whether you bother counting the cards or not.
REASON: You dismissed my warning about the odds.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas catches the censer in his bony palm, watching his lagging shadow stretch across the grass.
SAY: Keep your cards close then, friend, I'll just watch the rim.
TALK act1
NARRATOR: Silas sits close to the blaze, scraping grey river-tar and train soot from his ribs with a thumbnail while his censer swings.
SAY: Bit of a rough landing on the Ghostlight Express, eh, friend, rattles the whole cage right down to the heel-bones.
SAY: Back on Kalero's landings, when the sky went dark at least the lamps came on and you knew which alley held the knife.
SAY: Here we've got endless night and that giant Crooked Moon grinning down like a landlord waiting on a late tab.
SAY: Packed my brass grate full of bitter wormwood the second we crawled out of the wreck, just to keep the draught out of my teeth.
SAY: My little shadow's been lagging a half-step behind me ever since we hit Wickermoor Hollow, nervous as a cutpurse in church.
SAY: Still, the bone deck came through without a scratch, and my fingers work fine.
SAY: Whatever's running the tables in this valley, they haven't taken our buy-in yet.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up after the crash?
OPTION 2: This valley has all of us on edge.
OPTION 3: Get some rest while the fire's warm.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He taps two bony fingers against his breastbone, where the green pinpoints in his eye sockets flare bright.
SAY: Still in one piece, more or less, though my collar-bone's singing a sour note whenever the wind shifts.
SAY: Give me a dry spot by the ashes and a mark to hustle tomorrow, and I'll be right as rain, friend.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up after the crash.
REPLY 2
SAY: Good to know I'm not the only one hearing footsteps in the fog, because a lone hustler is an easy meal.
SAY: Stick close to the smoke, friend, and we'll watch each other's blind side till we figure the rules out.
REASON: You shared your own nerves on our first night.
REPLY 3
SAY: Catching forty winks under that moon is a tall order, friend, but I'll rest my eyes and keep one ear on the brush.
REASON: You told me to get some rest after the crash.
TALK act2
NARRATOR: Silas deals three bone cards face-up onto a flat stone by the fire, whistle-breathing through his teeth as the smoke curls.
SAY: Been thinking about that wreck on the tracks and the state of us after clearing out the Crooked House.
SAY: Most crews I ran with in Kalero would've split the loot and bolted for the tall grass the first time the walls bled.
SAY: We take a beating in this Hollow, spit out the grave-dirt, and walk right back to the table for another draw.
SAY: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and lately the monsters are the ones twitching when you lot step through the door.
SAY: Even my lagging shadow's stopped flinching at the tree-line, though it still tries to palm the best seat by the coals.
SAY: Never put much stake in partners who weren't taking a cut off the top.
SAY: Turns out having three solid backs around the fire beats a sleeve full of shaved aces any night.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up out here?
OPTION 2: We've all kept each other alive.
OPTION 3: Get some rest before the next stretch.
REPLY 1
SAY: Lighter on bitter herb than I'd like, and the damp in Wickermoor Hollow makes my knuckles click when I shuffle.
SAY: Better than I've been in four winters, though, and that's no bluff.
REASON: You checked on me deep in the Hollow.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Silas sweeps the bone cards back into one palm with a neat snap, his green eye-lights steadying on yours.
SAY: Put that in the ledger in clean ink, friend, because it's the only honest tab I've ever been glad to carry.
SAY: House comes calling for any of us, they'll have to clear the whole bench first.
REASON: You said we kept each other alive.
REPLY 3
SAY: Always the sensible play with you, friend, so I'll banking the grate and let the bones warm through.
REASON: You told me to rest while we had the fire.
TALK act3
NARRATOR: Silas sits with his knees drawn up and his brass censer dark in his lap, lettin' the firelight catch the nicks on his ribs.
SAY: Feel that hush sitting over the Hollow tonight, friend, like the whole room's holding its breath before the last card flips.
SAY: Spent my whole life hunting the cheap exit, shaving the rims, waiting for the moment to slip out the back with the pot.
SAY: Funny thing is, we're down to the final draw now and my boots aren't even itching for the door.
SAY: Look at us, battered as old dockside pilings, and still ready to double down against whatever's waiting in the dark.
SAY: House always wins, unless you burn the house, and I reckon we've got just enough spark left to try.
SAY: Whatever my old landlord's got written on my page, he didn't figure on me sitting at a table with you lot.
SAY: Win or fold tomorrow, friend, it's been a proper privilege running this shoe with you.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up before the end?
OPTION 2: No matter the draw, we finish it together.
OPTION 3: Get some rest while we still have tonight.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: His jaw gives a soft click, and for a second the rapid dockside patter drops right out of him.
SAY: Rattled down to the marrow, if you want the bare truth, friend, because you can't palm your way out of the last hand.
SAY: Still, my grip's steady enough to see the turn through with you.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up before the end.
REPLY 2
SAY: There's the stake that breaks the bank, friend, plain and straight on the baize.
SAY: Let the night bring its whole crooked deck, we'll meet it at the door.
REASON: You promised we would finish the last hand together.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Silas hooks the cool censer back onto his belt and stretches his bony legs toward the coals.
SAY: Best advice on the road, friend, I'll save my breath for the morning's buy-in.
REASON: You told me to rest before the final stretch.
